questions.stem: Which statement gives the most complete definition of biodiversity?

options.text: The variety of life at genetic, species and ecosystem levels
options.why: Biodiversity includes variation within species, among species and among ecosystems. Counting species covers only one part.

options.text: The number of species identified within a defined habitat during a survey
options.why: That describes species richness. It leaves out genetic variation, relative abundance and ecosystem diversity.

options.text: The genetic differences between individuals belonging to one population
options.why: That describes genetic diversity within a population. Biodiversity also operates at species and ecosystem levels.

options.text: The number of ecosystems that remain unaffected by human activity
options.why: That narrows ecosystem diversity to undisturbed sites. Modified ecosystems can still differ, and biodiversity includes two other levels.

questions.stem: What comparison between present and past species diversity is supported by the syllabus evidence?

options.text: Fossils prove that every modern species existed earlier in Earth’s history
options.why: Fossils show past organisms, not that every modern species already existed. Species appear through speciation and disappear through extinction.

options.text: Current species diversity is known exactly because all major habitats have been surveyed
options.why: Many living species haven’t been discovered or described. Taxonomic decisions also change the number recognized.

options.text: Fossil evidence suggests more species may live today than at any previous time
options.why: That’s the supported comparison, although the incomplete fossil record and unknown living species make exact counts impossible.

options.text: Past diversity always exceeded present diversity because five mass extinctions occurred
options.why: Mass extinctions caused major losses, but diversity recovered through later speciation. Their occurrence doesn’t establish a higher past total.

questions.stem: Two taxonomists examine the same populations, but the splitter reports more species than the lumper. Why?

options.text: The splitter counts every individual as a separate species
options.why: Splitters still classify groups of organisms as species. They don’t turn individual variation into one species per organism.

options.text: The splitter treats smaller differences as species boundaries
options.why: Splitters divide variation among more species, while lumpers include more of that variation within fewer species.

options.text: The lumper excludes extinct species from every biodiversity estimate
options.why: Lumping concerns where species boundaries are drawn. It doesn’t mean fossil species are automatically excluded.

options.text: The lumper measures evenness while the splitter measures richness
options.why: Both are making taxonomic classifications. Richness and evenness are separate measures used in community surveys.

questions.stem: Which explanation best describes the anthropogenic extinction of the North Island giant moa?

options.text: Introduced seals ate moa eggs while commercial fishing removed the birds’ food
options.why: That mixes unrelated marine pressures into a terrestrial case. Moas were large herbivorous birds hunted by people.

options.text: Climate cooling alone removed the forests before humans reached New Zealand
options.why: The required case concerns anthropogenic extinction. Human hunting and vegetation clearance were the relevant pressures.

options.text: Human hunting combined with burning and clearance of the birds’ habitat
options.why: People directly killed moas and also reduced their habitat. Together those pressures drove the populations to extinction.

options.text: Captive breeding reduced genetic diversity until the wild population disappeared
options.why: Moas weren’t lost through a conservation breeding program. This option reverses the historical situation.

questions.stem: Which pressure directly contributed to the extinction of the Caribbean monk seal?

options.text: Hunting for oil, meat and skins, combined with conflict with fisheries
options.why: People exploited the seals directly, and fishing added pressure through killing and reduced prey availability.

options.text: Forest clearance for oil-palm plantations in the seal’s nesting habitat
options.why: Oil-palm conversion is associated with Southeast Asian forest loss. Caribbean monk seals were marine mammals.

options.text: Commercial collection of seeds from wild seal breeding colonies
options.why: Seeds have no role in this animal extinction. Seed collection and seed banks concern plant material.

options.text: Suppression of natural fires across the seal’s grassland habitat
options.why: Fire suppression can alter grasslands such as prairie. It doesn’t describe a Caribbean marine habitat.

questions.stem: Which observation describes ecosystem loss rather than the extinction of one species?

options.text: The final individual of a captive bird species dies
options.why: That’s global species extinction because no living members remain. It says nothing about loss of an entire ecosystem.

options.text: One frog population disappears, but other populations survive
options.why: That’s a local extinction. The species survives elsewhere, and a whole ecosystem hasn’t necessarily been lost.

options.text: A forest is cleared for plantations, losing its communities
options.why: Conversion replaces the ecosystem’s physical habitat, biological community and interactions. Many species can be affected together.

options.text: A rare allele disappears from one isolated mammal population
options.why: That’s a reduction in genetic diversity. It concerns variation within a species rather than ecosystem loss.

questions.stem: Which study would provide the strongest evidence that biodiversity has declined over time?

options.text: One detailed species list made at a highly diverse site
options.why: A single list describes one time. Without an earlier or later comparable survey, it can’t demonstrate change.

options.text: Repeated comparable surveys showing declines across many habitats
options.why: Repeated measurements establish change, and agreement across habitats makes a broad crisis more credible than one local result.

options.text: A record showing that deforestation occurred near one protected reserve
options.why: Deforestation is a potential cause of biodiversity loss. This record doesn’t measure whether richness or evenness changed.

options.text: An estimate of how many species remain undiscovered worldwide
options.why: That estimate concerns uncertainty in the present total. It doesn’t track a change through time.

questions.stem: Why is human population growth described as an overarching cause of the biodiversity crisis?

options.text: It changes every ecosystem directly without requiring any human activity
options.why: Population size acts through activities and resource demands. The biological pressure still needs a mechanism.

options.text: It raises demand that intensifies habitat loss and overexploitation
options.why: Greater demand for land and resources can strengthen several direct pressures at once, which makes population growth overarching.

options.text: It prevents natural selection from occurring in all managed populations
options.why: Natural selection can continue in managed and wild populations. This doesn’t explain the broad biodiversity pressures.

options.text: It raises species richness by transporting organisms between continents
options.why: Transport can spread invasive alien species, pests and diseases. A local arrival can disrupt communities rather than conserve biodiversity.

questions.stem: A threatened predator can survive only where it hunts natural prey across a large territory. Which approach best preserves those interactions?

options.text: Store tissue samples without protecting any living population
options.why: Tissue storage preserves genetic material, not hunting behavior, prey relationships or a functioning population.

options.text: Keep the entire population permanently in a small zoo enclosure
options.why: That’s ex situ conservation and may prevent immediate extinction, but it can’t preserve the predator’s natural territory and interactions.

options.text: Protect and manage sufficient connected habitat in situ
options.why: In situ conservation can maintain the predator, its prey, natural behavior and ecological relationships within the habitat.

options.text: Preserve seeds collected from plant species in its habitat
options.why: A seed bank may protect plant genes, but it doesn’t maintain the predator’s territory, prey population or behavior.

questions.stem: What can a seed or tissue bank preserve most directly?

options.text: Natural food webs and competition between wild species
options.why: Those interactions require living communities in functioning habitats. Stored material can’t reproduce an active food web by itself.

options.text: Genetic material for possible future breeding or reintroduction
options.why: Stored germ plasm preserves alleles in seeds, cells or tissues that may later contribute to new organisms.

options.text: Learned migration routes followed by an animal population
options.why: Migration routes may depend on behavior, learning and habitat. They aren’t stored in a tissue bank.

options.text: Ongoing natural selection within an intact ecosystem
options.why: Stored material isn’t reproducing in its natural environment. Natural selection and ecological interactions aren’t maintained there.

questions.stem: Which action is an example of rewilding rather than reclamation?

options.text: Removing pollutants and rebuilding soil on a damaged industrial site
options.why: That’s reclamation because people are actively repairing physical conditions in a degraded site.

options.text: Collecting seeds from a rare plant for long-term cold storage
options.why: That’s ex situ germ-plasm storage. It preserves genetic material outside the ecosystem.

options.text: Reintroducing a missing native grazer to restore ecological processes
options.why: Rewilding restores natural processes, and reintroducing a missing native species can allow those processes to resume.

options.text: Breeding an endangered bird under controlled conditions in a zoo
options.why: That’s ex situ conservation. The organism is managed outside its natural habitat.

questions.stem: Four species face some extinction risk. Which one would receive the highest EDGE priority?

options.text: A vulnerable species with many closely related species
options.why: Its extinction risk matters, but many close relatives indicate lower evolutionary distinctness than an isolated lineage.

options.text: A secure species that is the sole member of an ancient lineage
options.why: It has high evolutionary distinctness, but low global endangerment. EDGE combines both criteria.

options.text: A critically endangered species from a long, isolated evolutionary branch
options.why: This species combines high global endangerment with high evolutionary distinctness, so its loss would remove unusually unique history.

options.text: An endangered species selected because it attracts the most public attention
options.why: Public appeal isn’t one of the two EDGE criteria. Priority depends on global endangerment and evolutionary distinctness.
